prompt: BLUNDER
explanation: A blunder is a clumsy error — the wrong name on an invitation, the wrong turn at a junction — and "mistake" names it directly. "Bargain" is a purchase made cheaply, "journey" a trip taken, and "promise" an undertaking given; a person can do all three without getting anything wrong.

prompt: STERN
explanation: A stern teacher or a stern warning allows no slack, which is what "strict" says. "Joyful" names a cheerful mood, "anxious" a worried one, and "modest" an unwillingness to boast; a teacher may be any of the three and still let every rule slide.

prompt: SOOTHE
explanation: To soothe a crying child or an aching shoulder is to ease the distress, which is what "comfort" does. "Scatter" spreads things apart, "measure" only finds out how much there is, and "flatter" works on a person's vanity rather than on what is hurting; none of the three makes anything hurt less.

prompt: SCARCE
explanation: Water in a drought or tickets on the last night are scarce — there is very little to be had, which is the sense of "rare." "Loud" describes sound, "damp" describes moisture, and "calm" describes stillness; a thing can be all three and still be piled to the ceiling.

prompt: QUAINT
explanation: A quaint cottage or a quaint custom pleases precisely because it is old-fashioned and a little out of step, and "charming" carries that pleasing quality. "Enormous" speaks to size, "reckless" to carelessness, and "alarming" to the fright a thing gives; a cottage may be any of the three and please no one.

prompt: HINDER
explanation: Deep snow hinders a rescue party by getting in its way and slowing it down, which is what "obstruct" names. "Postpone" puts the attempt off to a later hour without standing in anyone's path once it starts, "persuade" works on someone's mind, and "announce" only makes a thing known.

prompt: TRIVIAL
explanation: A trivial objection or a trivial scratch is too small to be worth the fuss, and "slight" names that smallness. "Hidden" says only that no one has seen it, "recent" says when it happened, and "narrow" describes its width rather than its importance — a scratch can be recent, hidden and narrow and still ruin the paintwork.

prompt: SCORN
explanation: To speak of a rival with scorn is to treat him as beneath serious notice, which is exactly "contempt." "Devotion" is loyal attachment, "jealousy" resentment of what another has, and "surprise" the effect of the unexpected; a man may envy a rival, or be startled by him, without once looking down on him.

prompt: LURE
explanation: Bait on a hook or the smell of bread from a doorway lures — it draws a creature or a customer in, which is what "attract" means. "Forgive" cancels a wrong, "inspect" examines closely, and "deliver" carries something to where it is wanted; none of the three brings anyone nearer of its own accord.

prompt: ELOQUENT
explanation: An eloquent speaker finds the words that carry an audience, and "articulate" names that command of expression. "Apologetic" describes a speaker's stance toward a fault, "deliberate" the unhurried care with which he proceeds, and "occasional" how often he speaks at all; a speaker may be all three and still never find the right word.

prompt: ZEAL
explanation: Zeal is the burning eagerness that keeps a volunteer at the work long after the others have gone home, and "fervor" names that heat. "Clamor" is loud noise, "tremor" a shaking, and "splendor" magnificence of appearance; a cause can be attended by all three and still find no one who cares about it.

prompt: WHIMSICAL
explanation: A whimsical design or a whimsical remark follows a passing fancy rather than a plan, and "playful" names that lightness. "Tactful" describes care not to give offense, "fearful" describes dread, and "mournful" grief; a remark can be tactful and still be made in dead earnest.

prompt: AFFABLE
explanation: An affable host puts strangers at ease within a minute of the door opening, which is what "friendly" names. "Wealthy" describes means, "worldly" wide experience of the world, and "truthful" a refusal to lie; a host may be all three and still leave his guests cold.

prompt: CLANDESTINE
explanation: A clandestine meeting is arranged so that no one outside it learns it happened, and "secretive" names that concealment. "Impulsive" says it was got up on the spur of the moment, "traditional" that it is held every year, and "elaborate" that a great deal of trouble went into it; a meeting can be all three and still be announced on a poster.

prompt: DEARTH
explanation: A dearth of rain or a dearth of qualified applicants means there is nowhere near enough of the thing, which is what "shortage" says. "Hardship" is what a shortage may cause rather than the shortness itself, "reminder" is something that prompts the memory, and "mixture" a combination of parts.

prompt: The first issue of the school paper was typed the night before it went out, and the staff counted four misspelled names on the front page alone; the second issue, by contrast, was -------.
explanation: Four misspelled names on a paper typed the night before mark work done in a rush, so the issue set against it must be the one put together with attention: "careful." "Crowded" speaks to how much was packed onto the page, "colorful" to how it looked, and "ambitious" to how much the staff tried to take on — a paper can be all three and still misspell four names.

prompt: Six winters, two moves, and a season spent out under the rain had not put a single crack in the frame, and Wei went on riding the same ------- bicycle to school every morning.
explanation: A frame that comes through six winters and a season in the rain without cracking is one that can be counted on, which is "dependable." "Handsome" and "fashionable" both describe how the bicycle looks to other people, and "expensive" what it cost; a bicycle can be all three and still crack in its first winter.

prompt: The seed library asked every borrower to return twice what was taken, and after four summers the shelves held more envelopes than the little room could store; by the one measure its founders had set, the arrangement was -------.
explanation: The founders' measure was the return of seed, and four summers later the shelves are overflowing, so the arrangement has done the work it was set up to do: "effective." "Wasteful" would mean the seed went nowhere, which is the opposite of shelves that will not hold it; "permissive" says only that borrowers were left to take what they liked, and "voluntary" that no one was made to take part at all.

prompt: The fog came in so thickly that the lighthouse beam reached no further than the end of the pier, and the harbormaster called the evening crossing -------.
explanation: When the light cannot be seen past the pier, a boat leaving the harbor cannot see what it is heading into, and that is what makes the crossing "unsafe." "Costly" speaks to the fare, "tedious" to how dull the trip is, and "popular" to how many want to make it; fog thick enough to swallow a lighthouse beam decides none of those.

prompt: Because the courtroom stenographer had to set down every word at the pace it was spoken, and because falling behind by even a phrase meant losing the one after it, ------- mattered to her more than any other part of the craft.
explanation: Keeping up with speech as it happens, where one phrase lost costs the next one too, is a demand on how fast she can work: "quickness." "Tidiness" would matter if the transcript had to look well kept, "modesty" concerns how she carries herself, and "imagination" would be called on only if she had to supply something of her own — the sentence names none of those difficulties.

prompt: The survey stakes planted at the ice edge in 1961 now stand more than a kilometer from it, so what the first crews recorded as a fixed boundary of the valley has proved ------- instead, and the stakes are the measure of it.
explanation: A boundary that has moved a kilometer within the life of one set of stakes was real enough but did not stay, and "temporary" is the word for that. "Illusory" would mean the crews had seen an edge that was never there, when the stakes show they planted them at one; "decorative" would mean it served no purpose, and "hazardous" that it was dangerous to approach.

prompt: Ngozi's program went out at two in the morning on a station that reached three counties, and in eleven years fewer than a dozen listeners ever wrote in; her audience, whatever its devotion, was -------.
explanation: Three counties, a two o'clock hour, and a dozen letters in eleven years all point at how few people were listening: "small." "Fickle" would mean they came and went, "aging" would describe their years, and "surly" their temper — and the sentence has already granted them their devotion.

prompt: The old shoemaker let his apprentice do nothing but watch for two years before he put a knife in her hand, and even then she was allowed only to cut linings, a ------- method he never explained and never defended.
explanation: Two years of watching, then a knife, then linings and nothing more marks a training let out in small stages, which is "gradual." "Generous" would describe how much he gave her and "cruel" how he treated her, while "settled" would mean only that the method was long since fixed — none of the three says the work was handed over a piece at a time.

prompt: Beginners kept asking the club the same three questions all season, proof enough that the instructions posted by the door were -------, and at the September meeting the committee voted to ------- them.
explanation: Newcomers who have read the notice and still ask the same three questions have not been told what they needed to know, and the remedy for that is new wording: "unclear ... rewrite." "Outdated ... replace" puts the fault in the passage of time, which three standing questions do not show; "lengthy ... shorten" blames the length when the questions suggest too little was said rather than too much; and "informal ... formalize" faults the tone, which is not what leaves a beginner in the dark.

prompt: Ridley expected the pigeons to break in every direction when the hawk crossed the square, but the flock held its shape and even drew tighter, a response he could only call -------, from birds he had spent years dismissing as a rabble.
explanation: A flock that keeps its shape and tightens under a hawk is behaving with an arrangement Ridley never expected from a rabble, and "orderly" names it. "Frantic" is what he expected and did not get, "leisurely" would make the birds slow when they drew tighter at once, and "routine" would say the behavior was ordinary — the sentence gives it as the opposite of what years of watching had taught him.

prompt: Bassani's version keeps every line break, every comma, and the word order of the original even where Italian syntax turns strange in English; whatever else it may be, his translation is ------- to a degree that unsettles some readers.
explanation: Holding to line breaks, commas, and word order even where the result reads strangely is following the original word for word, which is what "literal" describes. "Fluent" would mean the English runs smoothly, which the strangeness rules out; "abridged" would mean material was cut, and this version keeps everything; and "anonymous" concerns whose name is on the title page.

prompt: A wrong entry here, a sour note there: the quartet's recordings from the 1970s are technically -------, and yet collectors pay far more for them than for the ------- studio versions the group made a decade later.
explanation: Wrong entries and sour notes are faults in the playing, and the sentence turns on collectors preferring those recordings to the later ones, which must therefore be the clean ones: "flawed ... immaculate." "Dated ... modern" makes the first failing a matter of age rather than of playing, "obscure ... celebrated" describes reputation instead of execution, and "brief ... expansive" describes length — none of the three accounts for a sour note.

prompt: The quota had been fixed from the catch of a single exceptional year and was never revised afterward, which meant that a boat obeying the law to the letter could still be -------.
explanation: A limit set from the best year on record lets boats take more than an ordinary year can spare, so a captain can stay inside the law and still do harm to the stock: "destructive." "Lucrative" says how the season pays, "inefficient" how much is wasted in the taking, and "conspicuous" how visible the boat is — none of the three is what an over-generous limit produces.

prompt: Halvorsen published nothing, corresponded with no one at the observatory, and left his forty notebooks to a nephew who sold them for scrap paper; the record of his years at the eyepiece is therefore -------.
explanation: Nothing was published and nothing was sent to anyone, so the notebooks were the whole of the record, and the notebooks went out as scrap: "destroyed." "Disputed" would require a record for someone to argue over, "reprinted" one that reached a press, and "admired" one that readers had seen.

prompt: Every measure the town council passed that year opened with a paragraph explaining where the previous council's version had gone wrong, so the year's statute book reads less like a body of law than like a series of -------.
explanation: Each law begins by arguing against the law it replaces, and a run of texts whose business is answering earlier claims is a series of "rebuttals." "Concessions" would mean the new council gave ground to the old one when it is doing the opposite, "forecasts" look ahead rather than back, and "inventories" merely list what is held.
